analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal tax on capital gains and stock dividends for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have eliminated capital gains and dividend taxes for a decade, never received a hearing or vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee at the end of the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the tax code so that, for ten years, individuals would pay no federal income tax on capital gains (profits from selling stocks, real estate, or other assets) or on qualified stock dividends. Corporate taxpayers would still pay. Most capital gains and dividend income flows to higher-income households, so the tax break would be concentrated among investors, and the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers, borrowing, or spending cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors with taxable capital gains and stock dividends. Under current law those earnings are taxed at preferential rates (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income); this bill would cut that rate to zero for ten years. Because capital gains and dividends are heavily concentrated among wealthier households, the benefit would flow overwhelmingly to them — a household with no investments would see no direct benefit at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors with capital gains and dividends

how_it_helps.text: Allows taxpayers other than corporations to exclude their entire net capital gain from gross income for tax years 2012 through 2021, cutting the tax on asset sales to zero [S2][S3].
Treats qualified dividend income as part of net capital gain for purposes of the exclusion, so stock dividends also become tax-free for the ten-year window [S2][S3].
Suspends the special capital-gains rate schedule and the alternative minimum tax treatment of capital gains for those years, so investors pay no alternative tax on investment income either [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone else, indirectly. All the federal revenue now raised from capital gains and dividend taxes would disappear for a decade, so the government would either collect more in other taxes, borrow more, or spend less. Wage earners would also pay a higher effective tax rate on their labor income than investors pay on investment income, since wages would remain fully taxed.

drawbacks.text: The exclusion would eliminate all federal revenue from capital gains and dividend taxation for ten years, a very large revenue loss that would have to be offset by other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts [S2][S3].

Because capital gains and dividends are concentrated among higher-income households, the tax cut would go mostly to investors while households earning wages would continue paying full tax on their income, widening the gap between how work and investment income are taxed.

A zero rate on asset sales creates a strong incentive to recharacterize ordinary income (such as compensation or interest) as capital gains, inviting tax avoidance strategies that shift the burden onto other taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a large, certain tax cut to investors while imposing a broad, diffuse cost on everyone else through lost revenue and a widened preference for investment income over wages. A household living on wages gets nothing directly and shares the fiscal cost. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge the ten-year, unlimited exclusion is far larger and less targeted than narrower proposals like reducing rates or exempting small gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Stephen Fincher introduced the bill on September 12, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The Ways and Means Committee held no markup or vote, and the full House never considered the bill; the only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S5].
With no floor vote in either chamber, the bill expired with the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from passage because nothing passed; taxpayers generally are better off that the decade-long exemption of investment income from tax never became law, and no investor received the benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers generally; the cut never passed

for.name: Rep. Stephen Fincher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 12, 2011, and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only support on record was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: High-income investors and households with capital gains and dividends
industries.note: The bill would cut their tax rate on capital gains and qualified dividends to zero for ten years. Because that income is concentrated among wealthier households, the benefit would accrue mainly to them while the lost revenue is spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Financial services industry (brokerages, mutual funds, asset managers)
industries.note: A zero tax rate on asset sales and dividends would make taxable investing more attractive, potentially boosting trading and fund business. The gain is speculative and smaller than the direct benefit to investors themselves.

industries.industry: Federal treasury and public programs funded by general revenue
industries.note: The bill would eliminate a major revenue stream for a decade. Programs and services funded from general revenue, and everyone who relies on them, would bear the cost through cuts, other taxes, or borrowing.
